text:
The death toll from Hurricane Helene has reached at least 44 across four states
WASHINGTON (TND) — Hurricane Helene made landfall in Florida’s Big Bend region late Thursday night as a category 4 hurricane.
Though Helene was downgraded to a tropical storm Friday morning, it continues to have historic and devastating impacts as it makes its way up through the southeast.
As of 4 p.m. EDT, at least 44 people were reported dead in four states, according to The Associated Press.
There were at least 11 storm-related deaths in Georgia alone, including a first responder, Gov. Brian Kemp said during a news conference.
"At this time, this has been a deadly storm. We've had 11 confirmed fatalities," the governor said. "I would ask all Georgians like the Kemp family's doing to keep these folks in these communities, in your thoughts and prayers, we know that one of those was a first responder. When we ask people to stay off the roads and be patient, is because we are trying to get to people. It is a very dangerous environment, and one of our finest has lost his life trying to save others."
People from surrounding states have also been killed, authorities said. One Floridian died when a sign fell on their car, and three people were killed by toppled trees in the Carolinas.
South Carolina
In South Carolina alone, over a million customers were left without power Friday morning and winds reaching 60 mph whipped across the midlands.
Down trees and flooded roadways prompted emergency rescues, according to our member station WACH.
The risk of flash flooding is over, but river water is still rising to flood stage, according to WACH.
North Carolina
North Carolina, already dealing with the effects of historic rainfall Wednesday and Thursday, is braced for a third consecutive record breaking precipitation in Asheville as Helene hits the Tar Heel state in earnest Friday.
Multiple counties are under flash flood warnings and some are under mandatory evacuation orders, according to WLOS. Hundreds of thousands of North Carolina’s are without power Friday morning.
Georgia
When passing over Georgia Thursday night and early Friday morning, Helene brought sustained winds of 70 mph as it was downgraded to a tropical storm. Some schools and airports closed Friday.
"This is going to be a multi-state event with the potential for significant impacts from Florida all the way to Tennessee," said Deanne Criswell with FEMA. "So, please take this threat from storm surge seriously. Residents that are in these areas, they can still take action. They can take action now to move out of harm's way."
Tennessee
More than 50,000 people are without power in Tennessee as of Friday morning, according to powerout.us.
As of Friday morning, some schools were closed in Tennessee, and the state still anticipates heavy rain and wind from Tropical Storm Helene, according to member station ABC 9.
Florida
Helene hit Florida as a category 4 hurricane with winds of 140 miles per hour and catastrophic storm surge around 11:10 Thursday night.
Friday, all tropical-related alerts have been canceled for Florida, according to WEAR.
